title: NFS: Shared Filesystems and How They Hang
intro: NFS lets many servers mount the same directory over the network. It's old, simple, and everywhere: shared uploads, home directories, and the 'ReadWriteMany' volumes in Kubernetes. Its failure mode is distinctive: when the server goes away, clients don't get an error, they freeze. The NFS server is nfs-1; you're on a client, web-1.

steps.prompt: See which directories nfs-1 offers, and to whom.
steps.explanation: Three exports: two limited to private ranges, and /export/scratch offered to everyone.
steps.why: An export is a directory plus a list of clients allowed to mount it. The '*' on scratch means any host that can reach the server. NFS (version 3 especially) trusts the client's address and the user ids it claims, so the export list and the network firewall are the access control. A world-readable export is one of the commonest findings in internal security scans.

steps.explanation: The remote directory now appears as a local path.
steps.why: A mount made by hand is gone after a reboot. Permanent mounts go in /etc/fstab or a systemd mount unit, with the '_netdev' option so the system waits for the network, and 'nofail' so that an unreachable NFS server doesn't stop the machine booting. An fstab line without those can leave a server stuck at start-up.

steps.prompt: Check the options the mount is actually using.
steps.why: 'hard' is the default and the important one. If the server stops answering, a hard mount retries for ever: every process that touches the mount blocks, uninterruptibly, until the server returns. That protects data (a write is never silently lost) and it's why an NFS outage looks like a frozen fleet rather than an error (servers-incident-007). 'soft' gives up with an I/O error instead, which is safer for availability and risks corrupting files being written.

steps.prompt: On the server side, the exports file was edited to restrict /export/scratch. Apply the change without restarting the NFS service. (You're now on nfs-1.)
steps.explanation: The server re-read /etc/exports and updated what it offers.
steps.why: 'exportfs -ra' re-exports everything from the file, live, with no interruption to existing clients. 'exportfs -v' shows the result with every option in force, which is worth checking: a space in the wrong place in /etc/exports ('host (rw)' instead of 'host(rw)') silently grants read-write to the whole world.

steps.prompt:
An export has the option root_squash, the default. What does it do?
  a) Compresses files owned by root
  b) Maps requests made as root on a client to an unprivileged user on the server, so that being root on a client doesn't make you root over the shared files
  c) Blocks root from mounting
  d) Deletes root's files
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
root_squash    : client uid 0 -> server 'nobody'   (default, keep it)
no_root_squash : client uid 0 -> server uid 0      (any client's root owns everything)
steps.hint: The server only sees a user id number that the client claims.
steps.explanation: Client root is demoted on the server.
steps.why: With classic NFS security the server believes the user id the client sends. root_squash at least stops a compromised or careless client's root from reading and changing every file on the share. It's also why containers running as root often 'can't write' to an NFS volume: they've been squashed to nobody. no_root_squash fixes that symptom by removing the protection; the better fix is the right ownership on the export. For real authentication NFSv4 uses Kerberos.
